doc.title: Bob Cranshaw interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Milt Hinton as role model and the New York studio scene of the late 1950s-60s
summary: Hinton gave him a bass bag; Cranshaw describes network studio orchestras, record dates around 53rd and Broadway, and the masters who kept young players away from drugs.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Now I want to come back in and say you said that there was a lot of things going on, a lot of trouble that a young man could get into. But the music and the masters of the music kept you away from it. Elaborate on that.

Well Milt Hinton was one of the masters. One of the things that was funny, when I came to New York I came, I had a decent bass, but I had a bass case that was so raggedy. I mean it was in bad shape. And I used to go to clubs until Milton looked at this bass case and he said, “Son, you can’t be going around with a case like this.” So he donated a, he gave me a bass bag. ‘Cause he was embarrassed. But it showed me, I mean he was just so, his demeanor at that time. When I came to New York, there was a lot of jobs. There was a lot of studio things happening. And every, ABC, CBS and NBC they all had studio orchestras. And so Clark Terry and a lot of these guys that a lot of people don’t know were in these bands. But the bands didn’t have T.V. shows to play, so they were kind of getting paid but they were doing all kinds of record dates. They would run from one studio, and it was really exciting. I used to stand right around the corner here on 53rd and Broadway, and just watch the guys run back and forth to the record dates, and you know, it was exciting. It was a very exciting time period. And that was in the late 50s and the 60s. It was just very exciting. You know all of the people, but Milt Hinton and Hank Jones and guys really were role models for the younger guys. There was a group who were already into what we were talking about the drugs. I mean that was a separate © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

situation happening. But the Milt Hintons and people like that they were just, they were wonderful. I mean Milt Hinton, I still, he’s just marvelous. He’s just a marvelous person. And I wanted to be Milt Hinton. I wanted to be this. The next Milt Hinton was my dream. I just wanted to be like he was. And Joe and Milt and all of them were very close. So hearing their experiences, trying to re-live some of the experiences that I had heard them talk about, and so forth, was just wonderful. And I think I caught maybe the tail end of a period that was just incredible. And the young guys now, we don’t have the same thing going. I feel kind of bad. Because we didn’t do the same. They did this for us and I don’t think we did the same for the kids who are coming up now, which I’m trying to make up because I’m trying to work more with young people and do more with the union and different situations. Because I understand a lot more of what is happening and things to be able to say to a younger musician coming up now. Because it’s very hard. It’s difficult. We have wonderful people coming out of colleges, but I don’t know where they’re going. I don’t know. The competition, you know — whether it’s classical music or whatever — the competition is fierce. It’s incredible. And there’s so many great players.
